title: Teaching on Purpose #4: Securing Whole-Class Attention
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: Adam Kohlbeck, writing from Chiltern Learning Trust, explores how whole-school routines for securing student attention interact with adaptive teacher expertise. Through an interview with Yamina Bibi, he examines the argument that a single, consistent call for attention -- such as '3,2,1 SLANT' -- creates culturally valuable predictability for students as they move between classrooms, while still leaving room for teachers to exercise individual judgement in complex situations. The article distinguishes between contexts where a shared routine adds most value (schools establishing norms) versus where experienced teachers may adapt signals to the moment. It concludes that teacher agency and whole-school consistency are not opposites -- shared frameworks succeed when staff understand the evidence behind them and believe in the problem they are solving.
points: A whole-school attention routine creates predictability and familiarity for students who move between many teachers each day, reducing cognitive load on the transition itself and helping students quickly reorient to learning.

The benefit of a whole-school call for attention is context-dependent: in schools establishing new behavioural norms it can be transformative; in schools with long-standing culture it reinforces existing expectations.

Individual teachers will still need more fine-grained attention moves -- such as minimally invasive cues (a hand on a desk, a strategically placed question during modelling) -- that a whole-school signal cannot cover.

Mandated approaches fail when staff are handed directives without understanding the underlying data and rationale; Kohlbeck endorses a structured explanation format: state the data, name the problem it represents, describe the collective action, and articulate the expected reward.
Adaptive expertise requires something stable to adapt from -- abandoning consistency in favour of individual variation at every level misunderstands how professional skill develops.
quotes: Whether you prefer more or less precision around a call for attention is not the important thing. The important thing is that you are working in a school in which you have belief in the expectation.
People tend to be quite happy with a whole school call for attention if there has been proper consultation around it and if they understand the problem they are trying to solve.
With teacher agency rightly high on the national agenda, we must be careful to not assume that any attempt to establish shared routines in a school is automatically a bad thing.
Adaptive expertise requires a sound grounding in something to be adapted from.

If every teacher is using '3,2,1 SLANT' as their call for attention then this creates an element of predictability and familiarity for students as they move from one teacher to the next. Everyone knows what is expected and how to meet those expectations.
Without these checks and resets for attention, the teacher risks simply performing to an audience.
